name: Pedro Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. Could you walk me through an ordinary shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the excavator team at a large gypsum mine and take the controls when the digging face gets awkward. Our big machine scoops ore into trucks, and I watch the wall for a fresh crack before the bucket swings. I have a two-year technical diploma and enough practice to know a clean drawing can miss a weak seam. My partner Ella sells vegetables at a market stall, our children are grown, and the house is paid off. We have fourteen months of expenses saved and hope I can retire at 64. I use AI now and then to tidy repair notes after the fitters have checked the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a quick repair note can save a fitter time. A quick repair note does not hold up a mine wall. I would keep the morning wall check exactly where it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my higher lead pay will continue, and Ella's market stall brings another income when trade is good. Fourteen months saved and no house loan make this mild picture comfortable for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the wall walk before the first truck and ask the fitter to show me errors in any new repair-note tool. In the first year I'll try the tool on old excavator fault notes only after that demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our income. A proven tool is welcome; a shiny one without a real test can wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What fault did you find before the repair sheet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month I heard a bucket tooth scrape differently and stopped to find a loose pin. The repair sheet had the old tooth count, so the fitter corrected it before we dug again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the retirement transfer change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Ella we can keep our usual retirement transfer and the visit to our grown children. A faster note does not mean I need another device at home.

say: I would welcome **quicker repair notes** after a fitter checks the machine.
I would keep the **morning wall check** before any excavator bucket swings.
think: I expect my **higher lead pay** and Ella’s market income to continue.
I think our **paid house** and fourteen months saved make this picture comfortable.
do: **Keep walking** the excavation wall before the first truck.
**Try the repair-note tool** on old faults after a fitter demonstrates its mistakes.
feel: **Calm** about income and willing to use a tested note tool.
S0.quote: A quick repair note does not hold up a mine wall.
fieldNote: His **wall check** and loose bucket pin show how physical faults can escape an old repair sheet.
He uses **AI occasionally** and waits for a fitter’s real test before trying a new tool.

steps.text: Keep inspecting the excavation wall before the first truck
Learn the AI repair-note tool after a fitter demonstrates its errors

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say buying and scheduling may change before a robot can work this excavator. If a new plan sends trucks too close to a weak wall, the operator must be able to refuse it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the planning office may need fewer people, and my team could be asked to fill more trucks each hour. My own wage looks safe, but I do not want a younger operator hurried under a cracked face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the fitter to show me the route-planning screen after the trial at our mine. In the first year I'll compare its proposed loading positions with three wall inspections and give wrong positions to the shift supervisor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel interested, and a little uneasy for newer drivers near the wall. We can afford a delayed load; an injured apprentice cannot be paid back with overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which loading position would you reject?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the screen puts a truck beside the south crack, I will stop the excavator and move the loading point. The excavator wall will not wait for a neat loading schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a new driver who disagrees?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a new driver to call out a bad position even if I signed the plan. Years of practice do not make me right every time.

say: I would expect **buying and scheduling** to change before robots work the excavator.
I would protect an **operator’s stop call** beside a weak wall.
think: I expect my **wage** to hold while the planning office changes.
I worry **higher truck targets** could rush younger operators near cracked ground.
do: **Learn the route screen** after the mine completes a real trial.
**Compare loading positions** with three wall inspections and report wrong ones to the supervisor.
feel: **Interested** in planning tools and uneasy about new drivers beside weak ground.
S1.quote: The excavator wall will not wait for a neat loading schedule.
fieldNote: He accepts **planning tools** after a site trial and checks positions against physical wall inspections.
His **own income feels safe**; the feared harm is a hurried apprentice near a crack.

steps.text: Learn the AI route screen after a site trial
Keep checking proposed loading positions against wall inspections

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team thinking AI by 2028 can write load plans, while capable excavator robots follow around 2031. A final year of excavator work still pays wages and pension contributions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when robots arrive, and I had planned to finish at 64. Fourteen months saved could cover that gap if nothing else goes wrong, but Ella's stall income changes with the season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the retirement office for written pension figures at 63 and 64 this month and add part of each bonus to our reserve. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'll apply for a posted wall-inspection shift if the mine offers one at pay close to my lead wage; otherwise I'll keep operating while shifts exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing the last year of work even with our savings. I have options, but I would rather earn it than spend down what we saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which family purchase would you delay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Ella we should delay replacing the market van until we see the retirement figures. The old van still runs, and her stall needs cash for vegetables every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make inspection work worth taking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether a wall-inspection post includes walking the face, not just signing photographs. I would take it only with the pay and real work stated in the offer.

say: I would distinguish **2028 load planning** from capable excavator robots around 2031.
I would ask for **written pension figures** before treating the last year as covered.
think: I think at **63**, robots could take my final working year before planned retirement at 64.
I think our **fourteen-month reserve** might bridge it, but Ella’s stall income is seasonal.
do: **Add bonus money** to our reserve after requesting pension figures at 63 and 64.
**Apply** for a posted inspection shift after thinking AI arrives only with near-lead pay and real wall checks.
**Delay the market van** replacement until written retirement figures arrive.
feel: **Anxious** about losing one final earning year despite savings and nearby work options.
S2.quote: A final year of excavator work still pays wages and pension contributions.
fieldNote: His **2031 age** is 63, just one year before planned retirement at 64.
His **inspection application** needs a posted shift, near-lead pay and real wall checks; seasonal stall income limits the bridge.

steps.text: Add part of each bonus payment to the household reserve
Apply for posted wall-inspection work if pay stays near lead wage and includes wall checks
Delay replacing the market van until retirement figures arrive
Request written pension figures for ages 63 and 64

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2031 changes load plans, while capable excavator robots arrive around 2034. By then I would be 66, two years beyond the age I hope to retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still need the lead wage to 64 and a pension that covers our usual bills. The paid house and fourteen months saved help, but I will not give notice before seeing the actual mine pension statement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep leading excavator shifts and ask the retirement office to update my pension statement each year. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'll choose a retirement date only if the written pension covers our regular bills without counting a good market season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the robot date and careful about the pension. I can take a little time to show the apprentices how a wall crack opens before I leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your shifts end before retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the mine cuts my shifts at 63, I'd apply for a posted excavator opening at a nearby mine. I would need an offer at workable pay, not just a vacancy notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you tell your partner a date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Ella the date when the pension and our house costs fit on the same page. Our grown children should hear a decision, not a guess.

say: I would see **2034 robots** after my hoped-for retirement at 64.
I would want **written pension income** before handing back the excavator keys.
think: I need **lead wages** through 64 and a pension covering regular bills.
I think the **paid house** and savings help, but I will not count a strong market season as certain.
do: **Keep leading** excavator shifts and seek annual pension statements.
**Set retirement date** after thinking AI arrives only if written pension covers bills without seasonal stall income.
feel: **Calm** about the robot date while careful about pension adequacy.
S3.quote: I will not give notice before seeing the actual mine pension statement.
fieldNote: His **2034 age** is 66, two years after intended retirement.
A **nearby excavator job** is a fallback only if shifts end before 64 and an actual workable offer arrives.

steps.text: Keep leading excavator shifts and requesting yearly pension statements
Set retirement date only if written pension covers bills without stall income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI by 2036 changes the office plan, while capable excavator robots arrive around 2039. If my pension holds, the machine date is for the younger operators to plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 when thinking AI arrives and 71 when robots come. Our paid house and fourteen months saved should let me finish at 64 if the written pension covers bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep operating carefully and paying into retirement while shifts last. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, if retired as planned, I'll check our pension budget with Ella and help the local trade school with one practical excavator lesson if it asks me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm for our own household, and I want apprentices to learn a real machine before a robot takes the seat. A video cannot teach the weight of an excavator bucket full of wet ore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if pension income is low?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the pension is low, I would take a posted excavator shift at a nearby mine before using the reserve. I would need an actual offer at workable pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show a trainee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the trainees to watch the wall as well as the bucket. The machine may change, but the ground can still fall.

say: I would expect **2039 excavator robots** after my planned retirement.
I would support **practical apprenticeships** on real machines.
think: I think at **68 and 71**, I expect retirement if written pension income covers bills.
I think our **paid house and savings** help but do not replace a pension.
do: **Keep operating** safely and paying into retirement while shifts last.
**Review pension bills** with Ella after 2036 if retired as planned.
**Teach one excavator lesson** at the trade school if it invites me.
feel: **Calm** about household security, with interest in teaching apprentices hands-on skills.
S4.quote: A video cannot teach the weight of an excavator bucket full of wet ore.
fieldNote: His **2036 and 2039 ages** are 68 and 71, beyond planned retirement.
He would teach a **trade-school lesson** only if asked, and would seek a real nearby offer if pension income falls short.

steps.text: Keep operating excavators and paying into retirement while shifts last
Review pension income against bills with Ella after 2036 if retired

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable excavator robots could arrive around 2031, one year before my planned retirement. A posted wall-inspection job at near-lead pay and written pension figures would help me choose without draining our reserve.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether a senior operator should teach the next one. A new excavator driver should learn to see a mine wall crack before watching a screen for one.

headlineQuote: A new excavator driver should learn to see a mine wall crack before watching a screen for one.
portrait: **Pedro Young**, 58, leads excavator work at a large gypsum mine after a two-year technical diploma.
His **higher lead pay**, paid house and fourteen months saved support retirement plans alongside his partner’s seasonal market stall.
He tries **AI occasionally** after fitters prove a tool and keeps inspecting walls and bucket parts himself.
He hopes to **retire at 64**, making 2031 robots at 63 a risk to one final earning year.
A **posted wall-inspection job** must pay near his lead wage and include real face checks before he applies.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because capable excavator robots could arrive one year before planned retirement.
whatWouldHelp: A **posted inspection job** at near-lead pay and written pension figures would protect the household reserve.
